g8-2023-008.lessonTitle: Finding Distances in the Coordinate Plane
g8-2023-008.quote: how to find the distance between any two coordinate pairs
g8-2023-008.why: The item gives two points as coordinates only, with no graph, and asks for the distance between them. This activity hands each student a pair of coordinates with no picture, has them calculate the distance, and then write out a general method.

g8-2023-019.quote: Reflect ABCD over the x -axis, then reflect its image over the y -axis
g8-2023-019.why: The item asks which sequence of transformations maps a triangle onto its congruent image on a coordinate plane. This activity's narrative names exactly that kind of answer - axis reflections composed with a translation - as the sequences students produce for congruent grid figures.

g8-2023-024.quote: translations, rotations, and reflections preserve side lengths and angle measures
g8-2023-024.why: The item asks what is always true of a segment after a reflection followed by a rotation; the answer is that it is congruent to the original. This activity is where students establish that rigid motions preserve length and angle.

g8-2023-025.quote: The diagram shows two parallel lines cut by a transversal
g8-2023-025.why: The item gives two angle expressions in a parallel-lines-and-transversal figure and asks for x; the equation comes from knowing the two angles are congruent. This Cool-down is where the curriculum tests deducing all angles in that exact figure from one known angle. Note the curriculum never labels those angles with algebraic expressions.

g8-2023-035.quote: no fractional representation exists for these numbers
g8-2023-035.why: The item asks students to say whether the square root of 50 is rational or irrational and why, with the correct reason stated in terms of a non-repeating, non-terminating decimal. This activity is where the curriculum makes that case, though it frames irrationality as 'no fraction exists' and reaches the endless decimal through successive approximation rather than stating the decimal test the item uses.

g8-2023-039.quote: the definition of a cube root as a solution to the equation
g8-2023-039.why: The item asks for the solution of x cubed = 125. This activity is built on exactly that form - students are given x cubed = 5, y cubed = 27, z cubed = 700 and must produce the values, with the perfect cube giving an integer.

g8-2023-040.quote: A right triangle has sides of length 2.4 cm and 6.5 cm
g8-2023-040.why: The item describes a right triangle in words only - right angle at F, legs 9 and 12 - and asks for the hypotenuse. This activity's problems are the same verbal, figure-free form, and the lesson is where students sort out which named side is the hypotenuse.

g8-2023-042.quote: Describe a sequence of reflections, rotations, and translations
g8-2023-042.why: The 2-credit item asks students to describe a sequence of transformations mapping one triangle onto its congruent image. This Cool-down asks for exactly that, in the same words, for a pair of grid quadrilaterals.

g8-2023-044.quote: The triangle has side lengths 7, 10, and 12
g8-2023-044.why: The 2-credit item gives three side lengths and asks whether the triangle is right, citing the Pythagorean theorem. This Cool-down is that question verbatim, with 'Explain your reasoning' - it is where the converse is tested.

g8-2024-004.lessonTitle: Parallel Lines and the Angles in a Triangle
g8-2024-004.quote: the measure of angle EAB equal to the measure of any angle
g8-2024-004.why: The item requires two moves: an angle of the image equals an angle of the original (rigid motion preserves angles), then the third angle is 180 minus the other two. This activity asks both - whether a rotated image's angle equals an angle of the original triangle, and what three such angles sum to.

g8-2024-012.quote: Decide mentally whether each statement is true
g8-2024-012.why: The item asks which value of x makes x cubed = 64 true, with 8 as the tempting wrong answer. This Math Talk asks students to judge the statement 'the cube root of 64 = 2' mentally - the same perfect-cube reasoning and the same square-versus-cube confusion.

g8-2024-019.quote: Translate EFGH 1 unit to the right, and then rotate its image 180 degrees
g8-2024-019.why: The item asks which reflection-then-rotation sequence maps a trapezoid onto its image. This activity's narrative gives the parallel example of a translation composed with a 180-degree rotation about (0, 0) as a sequence students produce here.

g8-2024-023.lessonTitle: Parallel Lines and the Angles in a Triangle
g8-2024-023.quote: why the sum of the three angles in a triangle is 180
g8-2024-023.why: The item asks for an expression, 180 - (x + y), for the third angle of a triangle. This activity is the general argument that any triangle's three angles sum to 180 with no numbers given, which is the fact the expression encodes. The curriculum never writes that fact algebraically.

g8-2024-030.quote: Is it a right triangle? Explain your reasoning
g8-2024-030.why: The item asks which of four lists of three numbers could be the sides of a right triangle, which means testing each triple against a squared plus b squared = c squared. This Cool-down asks exactly that question of one triple.

g8-2024-034.quote: On both figures, label all known side lengths and angle measures
g8-2024-034.why: The item asks which two sides of a rotated quadrilateral are equal in length, so students must match corresponding sides. This Cool-down asks students to label the corresponding known side lengths and angle measures on a figure and its image under a rigid transformation.

g8-2024-037.quote: the value of 2 is a bit less than 1.5
g8-2024-037.why: The item asks which statement best describes the square root of 2: between 1.0 and 1.5 but closer to 1.5. That is the stated purpose of this activity - students find the areas and side lengths of three squares and see the value is a bit less than 1.5.

g8-2024-040.quote: the side length of a square with each of the following areas
g8-2024-040.why: The item gives a square garden of area 324 square feet and asks for a side length. This Cool-down asks for the side length of a square given its area, mixing perfect squares with non-perfect ones.

g8-2024-041.lessonTitle: Finding Distances in the Coordinate Plane
g8-2024-041.quote: Calculate the exact lengths of segments e and f
g8-2024-041.why: The item shows a segment drawn on a coordinate plane and asks for its length, which requires building a right triangle on it. This Cool-down asks students to calculate the exact lengths of drawn coordinate-plane segments.

g8-2024-042.lessonTitle: Parallel Lines and the Angles in a Triangle
g8-2024-042.quote: the structure of parallel lines cut with a transversal to identify alternate interior angles
g8-2024-042.why: The 2-credit item has a triangle whose base lies on one of two parallel lines and asks for the apex angle, given the two angles where the transversals cross the other parallel line. That is this activity's figure and method: carry angles across the parallels, then use the 180-degree sum.

g8-2024-047.quote: Show that they are rational by writing them in the form
g8-2024-047.why: The 2-credit item gives a short list - a square root of a perfect square, a repeating decimal, a terminating decimal - and asks students to classify each and say how they know a number is rational. This activity's list has the same mix, including a square root, and asks for the same justification: write it as a fraction. The repeating-decimal member is settled one lesson later, in Unit 7 Lesson 17 'Some Numbers Are Rational'.

g8-2025-007.quote: How high up the utility pole does the support pole reach
g8-2025-007.why: The item gives a kite string of 20 feet as the slanted side and 15 feet along the ground, and asks which equation finds the vertical height. This Cool-down is the same situation - a slanted 11.5 m pole, 4.5 m along the ground, find the height - so students must place the given lengths as hypotenuse and leg.

g8-2025-015.quote: say what an irrational number is. Give at least two examples
g8-2025-015.why: The item asks which of four numbers must be removed so the set holds only rational numbers, i.e. spot the one irrational. This Cool-down is where students must state what rational and irrational mean and supply examples of each. Recognizing the repeating decimal in the set as rational is treated later, in Unit 7 Lesson 17.

g8-2025-017.quote: What is the image of two parallel lines under a rigid transformation
g8-2025-017.why: The item asks which sides of a translated rectangle are parallel - i.e. that a translation takes parallel segments to parallel segments. This activity has students translate a pair of parallel lines (3 up and 2 right) precisely to answer that question.

g8-2025-034.quote: is the image of trapezoid ABCD under a rigid transformation
g8-2025-034.why: The item asks which corresponding parts of a trapezoid and its 180-degree rotation are congruent, with distractors pairing the wrong vertices. This Cool-down has students label the corresponding sides and angles of a trapezoid and its image, which is the same correspondence work.

g8-2025-037.quote: rational approximations of irrational numbers to place both rational and irrational numbers
g8-2025-037.why: The item asks on which number line point P sits at the value of the square root of 4 plus the square root of 10, so students must approximate an irrational root and locate the total. This activity is where students use rational approximations to place square roots on a number line. The summing of two roots shows up only in the Math Talk that opens Unit 7 Lesson 11, which asks for the square root of 10 plus the square root of 97 to the nearest half.

g8-2025-042.quote: not all numbers written using square root or cube root notation are irrational
g8-2025-042.why: The item asks students to classify the square root of 1.44 as rational or irrational and justify it. This activity's values were chosen for precisely that point, and it asks students to show such numbers are rational by writing them as fractions.

g8-2025-047.quote: side lengths of the triangle and c is the longest side
g8-2025-047.why: The item shows squares drawn on the three sides of a 3-4-5 right triangle and a student who wrote 5 squared + 4 squared = 3 squared; students must find the error and give the correct steps. This Cool-down is where the theorem is stated with the condition the student broke - c is the longest side - and the squares-on-sides diagram is this lesson's own representation. The area proof itself is Unit 7 Lesson 8, 'Adding Up Areas'.

g8-2026-005.quote: how they might figure out a value for π using measurements of circles
g8-2026-005.why: The item asks which of 0, pi, the square root of 9, and one third is irrational. This activity is the one place in the unit that treats pi as an irrational number alongside the square root of 2, and the square root of a perfect square being rational is settled in the previous lesson.

g8-2026-007.quote: then the triangle must be a right triangle, and c must be its hypotenuse
g8-2026-007.why: The item asks which equation proves a 9-12-15 triangle is right, so students must recognize the converse statement in symbols with the longest side as c. This activity is where that statement is introduced and argued.

g8-2026-022.quote: students apply the definition of congruence to figures on a square grid
g8-2026-022.why: The item gives two congruent triangles by coordinates and asks which reflection-plus-translation maps one to the other. This activity is where students produce such sequences on a grid, using coordinates of corresponding points.

g8-2026-025.quote: Find two pairs of angles in the diagram that have the same measure
g8-2026-025.why: The item asks which angle of a rotated triangle is congruent to which angle of the original. This activity asks students to identify corresponding points under a rigid transformation and then name pairs of angles that have the same measure and say how they know.

g8-2026-029.quote: In the image, write the length of each side, in grid units
g8-2026-029.why: The item asks for the length of a side of a triangle after a translation, which is the length of the original side. This activity has students translate a polygon on a grid and write the length of each side of the image.

g8-2026-031.activity: Cutting Parallel Lines With a Transversal
g8-2026-031.quote: find the seven unknown angle measures in the diagram
g8-2026-031.why: The item gives one angle at each of two parallel lines cut by transversals and asks for a third by carrying an angle across the parallels and subtracting. This activity is where students deduce every unknown angle in a parallel-lines-and-transversal diagram from what they know.

g8-2026-033.quote: think about the meaning of the cube root symbol
g8-2026-033.why: The item asks which value of x makes x cubed = 8 true. This Math Talk has students decide mentally whether statements about cube roots of perfect cubes are true, which is the same evaluation.

g8-2026-035.quote: The field is 100 meters long and 80 meters wide
g8-2026-035.why: The item gives 12 miles north and 16 miles east of a home and asks the distance between the two destinations - a real-world hypotenuse across a right angle. This activity is the same move: two perpendicular sides of a field, find the diagonal straight across.

g8-2026-038.lessonTitle: Square Roots on the Number Line
g8-2026-038.quote: explain why a given approximation of the square root is reasonable or not
g8-2026-038.why: The item marks four points on a number line and asks which best approximates the square root of 10. This activity asks students to judge whether a given point is a good approximation for the square root of 3 and to find a better one.
